sentences.text: Revenue (net interest income plus noninterest income) rose from $96.6 billion in FY2016 to $182 billion in FY2025, a 7.3% CAGR [D5][D206].

The path was not smooth: net income fell 20.0% in FY2020 to $29.1 billion [D94][F25], then jumped 65.8% in FY2021 to $48.3 billion [D118][F26], and after a 21.9% dip in FY2022 [D142][F27] compounded at a 14.8% three-year rate to $57.0 billion in FY2025 [D334][F30].

The FY2020 decline came as the provision for credit losses reached $17.5 billion, 14.6% of revenue [X142][D88], while net interest income fell 4.7% on lower rates and deposit growth that could not be deployed [D100][P65].

The FY2023 step change was rate-driven: net interest income rose 33.8% to $89.3 billion [D174][F8], with the provision at $9.3 billion [X145] and noninterest expense up 14.5% on compensation, the FDIC special assessment and First Republic costs [D178][P42].

Net interest income grew faster than fees over the window, an 8.4% CAGR against 6.2% for noninterest income [F111][F112], lifting net interest income to 52.3% of revenue in FY2025 from 47.7% in FY2016 [D209][D8].
North America remains the concentration: 76.6% of revenue in FY2025 [D249], contributing just 0.2pp of growth that year [D251] as its revenue grew 0.3% [D250].
International was the FY2025 driver, with EMEA up 9.5% (+1.2pp) [D275][D276] and Asia-Pacific up 17.3% (+1.2pp) [D300][D301].

Firmwide, net interest income rose 3.1% to $95.4 billion on higher Markets net interest income, higher Card Services revolving balances and higher wholesale deposits, largely offset by deposit margin compression [D221][F10][P28].
Profit did not keep pace in FY2025: net income fell 2.6% [D214] while revenue rose 2.8% [D226], as noninterest expense grew 4.2% [D225].
Per-share growth outran net income over the window, EPS up 13.9% a year against 9.7% for net income [F115][F113], as diluted shares fell 3.4% in FY2025 alone [D224].
The efficiency ratio was 52.4% in FY2025 [D207], better than the 57.2% window median [D333] and near the 51.7% window low set in FY2024 [D331], and far below the 61.7% banks peer median [D337].

The FY2025 ratio worsened 0.7pp from FY2024 [D207][D184] as noninterest expense rose 4.2% to $95.6 billion on higher compensation, brokerage and distribution fees, auto lease depreciation and technology and marketing spend [D225][X137][P26].
Credit costs are the pressure point: the provision was 7.8% of revenue in FY2025 [D208], up from 6.0% in FY2024 [D185] and above the 6.0% peer median [D341].

The FY2025 provision of $14.2 billion reflected net increases in the loan and commitment portfolios, credit-quality changes on client-specific exposures, an update to loss assumptions on certain leveraged loans and estimated fraud losses, partly offset by the macroeconomic outlook [X147][P15].
Below the line, the 21.4% effective tax rate [D203] left net margin at 31.2% [D210], close to the 32.9% of FY2024 [D187].

For a bank, operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure: it was -$147.8 billion in FY2025 [F60], a -2.59x ratio to net income [D204], and has swung sign repeatedly across the window [F55][F56][F59].

The FY2025 outflow came from higher trading assets, higher securities borrowed, net loan originations held-for-sale and higher other assets, partly offset by net income and higher trading liabilities [P21].
Capital return is the better test: buybacks plus dividends of $48.2 billion in FY2025 [D205] were 84.6% of net income [F30], up from $33.6 billion in FY2024 [D182].
Return on average equity was 16.1% in FY2025 [D213], at the 100th percentile of the seven-bank peer group against an 11.8% median [D338][D339].
Shareholders' equity reached $362 billion [F110], up 5.1% [D220], on total assets of $4.42 trillion [F90] that grew 10.5% [D218].
Liquidity is ample but thinner: cash and equivalents fell 26.8% to $343 billion [D219][F100], and loans were 57.3% of deposits [D211], up from 55.0% in FY2024 [D188].

The cash decline was driven by Markets activities in CIB, higher investment securities, higher loans and cash deployment in Treasury and CIO, largely offset by higher deposits and long-term debt [P24].
Capital was returned through $31.6 billion of buybacks [X102] and $16.6 billion of dividends [X112], with no acquisitions in FY2025 [X117].

The metrics table's net income for FY2021 through FY2025 comes from the proxy statement's pay-versus-performance table, not the 10-K, and differs by up to 0.10% [R1][F30][X20]; the 10-K figure of $57.0 billion [X20] is the one to use where precision matters.
The gap is rounding, not a restatement, but it means small year-over-year changes in the table should be checked against the filed figure [R1].
FY2020 pretax income and tax were later restated, to $35.8 billion and $6.7 billion against the $35.4 billion and $6.3 billion used here [R2][R3][X63][X73].
That recast shifts the FY2020 tax rate by roughly a point, so the FY2020 margin comparison should not be read too finely [R2][R3].
Watch the efficiency ratio: a move back above the 57.2% window median [D333] from 52.4% [D207] would reverse the cost trend, reported in the FY2026 10-K's Firmwide overview.
Watch the credit-loss provision: holding above the 6.0% peer median [D341] from 7.8% of revenue [D208] would confirm rising credit costs, disclosed in the FY2026 provision discussion.

Watch net interest income: a return below the FY2024 level of $92.6 billion [F9] from $95.4 billion [F10] would signal deposit margin compression outweighing balance-sheet growth, in the FY2026 net interest income discussion.
Watch the allowance at 1.8% of loans [D212]: a move above the FY2020 peak of 2.9% [D92] would mark a genuine credit cycle, in the FY2026 allowance rollforward.
